Pressure or filter?

Time-averaged protection of a pressurised room or house, counting both filter leakage and wind-driven infiltration. Wind comes from 5 years of hourly records (2019–2023) at the airports of the 60 largest US metros.

Protection factor against overpressure

How it is calculated

For every hourly record (2-minute mean wind speed and direction at 10 m, and outdoor temperature) the model works out how much unfiltered air gets in, as a fraction f of the fan's filtered flow, and averages f over the period.

  1. Airport wind is converted to wind at 6 m in the chosen terrain (×0.93 open, ×0.64 suburban; ASHRAE Fundamentals ch. 24).
  2. Each wall's pressure is Cp(angle) × ½ρU², with Cp for the surroundings from AIVC Technical Note 44. Gusts add a random part with rms 0.2–0.5 × ½ρU² (An & Jung 2023), independent for each wall and the roof.
  3. The rest of the house settles at the pressure that balances its own leaks (walls 60%, ceiling 25%, floor 15%), including stack effect from the indoor–outdoor temperature difference.
  4. The fan pushes a fixed flow into the room, set by the calm-weather overpressure. That flow leaves through the outside-wall leaks and the house-side leaks, with Q = C·Δp0.65 for each. The room pressure is solved for each gust. Air comes in wherever the outside is at higher pressure than the room. House air counts as outdoor air.
  5. Room concentration / outdoor = (Pfilter + f) / (1 + f + (CADR + k·V)/Q). Protection factor is its inverse.

A room with a fixed-flow fan rises in pressure when wind pushes on its outside wall. If half the leaks are in that wall, nothing gets in until the wall is 2.9× the calm overpressure above the house interior. A whole house gets far less of this, so it needs about three times the overpressure. Not included: fans whose flow falls as room pressure rises, door openings, leaks on the suction side of the fan, and the wind on the fan's own intake. No one has measured this under real wind at PF 1000. The only direct test (NIOSH, Heitbrink et al. 2000) is consistent with the model. Weather data: NOAA Integrated Surface Database (ISD-lite), 2019–2023. Flow exponent 0.65 (Chan et al. 2013).
